title: The Untold Story of Joseph
paragraphs: The Untold Story of Joseph
There are some people in the Bible we admire too quickly.
We quote their victories. We celebrate their endings. We preach their promotions.
But we rarely sit inside their loneliness long enough to understand what obedience actually cost them.
Joseph is one of those people.

Because before the palace… there was betrayal. Before authority… there was abandonment. Before dreams were fulfilled… there was silence so heavy it probably felt like heaven itself had forgotten his name.
And maybe that is why this story still cuts so deep.
Because some of you know exactly what it feels like to obey God and still end up in a pit.
Some of you know what it feels like to be hated for something you never did.
To be misunderstood. To be isolated. To be thrown away by people you would have died for.
Joseph’s story is not just about dreams.
It is about surviving seasons where nothing around you looks like the promise God gave you.
And that is where most believers quietly break.
Genesis 37:3 says:
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children…”
The Hebrew phrase used here is:
“אָהַב” (ahav)
Meaning: not merely affection, but deep covenantal love, attachment, favor, relational devotion.
Jacob’s favoritism toward Joseph was visible. Painfully visible.
The coat given to Joseph was not merely colorful clothing.
The Hebrew description “כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים” (ketonet passim) likely described a long-sleeved royal garment associated with honor, distinction, and inheritance.
It represented status. Authority. Selection.
And sometimes the favor of God on your life becomes the reason people resent you.
Not because you hurt them.
But because your existence reminds them of what they refuse to surrender to God.
Joseph’s brothers did not hate him overnight. Jealousy grew slowly. Quietly. Like mold in darkness.
Genesis 37:4 says:
“They hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.”
The Hebrew wording is haunting.
“וְלֹא יָכְלוּ דַּבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם”
Literally: “They were unable to speak shalom to him.”
Shalom does not simply mean peace.
It means wholeness. Completeness. Harmony. Welfare.
Their hearts had become so corrupted by envy they could no longer release wholeness from their mouths.
Jealousy changes language.
People consumed by bitterness eventually lose the ability to speak life.
And some of you have been wounded by words spoken from spiritually sick hearts.
But Joseph’s story becomes even more devastating when God gives him dreams.
Not fantasies. Not ego trips. Dreams.
The Hebrew word is:
“חֲלוֹם” (chalom)
A revelatory dream. A divine communication.
Joseph did not invent the future God showed him.
God revealed it.
Yet revelation without maturity can create unnecessary wounds.
Joseph shared dreams before learning wisdom.
And sometimes young believers mistake revelation for readiness.
The brothers’ hatred intensified.
Genesis 37:11 says:
“And his brothers envied him…”
The Hebrew word:
“וַיְקַנְאוּ־בוֹ” (vayekanu-bo)
Carries the sense of burning jealousy. A consuming fire of resentment.
Envy is terrifying because it can make people justify evil while still believing they are right.
Eventually Joseph’s brothers strip him.
Not just physically. Emotionally. Relationally. Mentally.
Genesis 37:23:
“They stripped Joseph of his coat…”
Because the enemy always attacks identity before destiny.
Then comes the pit.
The Hebrew word:
“בּוֹר” (bor)
A cistern. An empty hole. A place associated with death, confinement, isolation, desperation.
And this is the part many sermons rush through.
Joseph was seventeen.
Seventeen.
Imagine the confusion.
Imagine screaming for help while hearing your own brothers debate whether you deserved to live.
Imagine watching the people you trusted eat bread while you cried inside a pit.
Genesis 37:25 says:
“And they sat down to eat a meal.”
One of the coldest verses in Scripture.
Joseph’s pain became background noise to people consumed by their own hardness.
Some of you know this pain.
You broke privately while everyone around you kept scrolling, laughing, posting, living.
But what is fascinating is this:
The pit was not the end.
It was transportation.
Because sometimes God allows burial-looking seasons that are actually preparation.
Joseph is sold into slavery.
The Hebrew word for slave:
“עֶבֶד” (eved)
A servant. A bondman. Someone owned.
The dreamer became property.
Can you imagine the emotional violence of that transition?
One moment favored son. Next moment chained merchandise.
And still… God never abandoned him.
Genesis 39:2 repeatedly says:
“The LORD was with Joseph.”
The Hebrew:
“וַיְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף”
YHWH hayah et Yosef.
God was with him in slavery. God was with him in false accusation. God was with him in prison.
Notice: The presence of God did not prevent suffering.
This modern idea that favor guarantees comfort is biblically bankrupt.
Sometimes God’s presence is most visible in endurance.
Joseph prospers inside Potiphar’s house.
Then temptation comes.
Potiphar’s wife repeatedly pressures Joseph sexually.
Genesis 39:9 records Joseph saying:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
The Hebrew word for wickedness:
“רָעָה” (ra’ah)
Moral evil. Corruption.
Notice Joseph did not define sin by culture. By opportunity. By secrecy. By desire.
He defined it by God.
Modern culture says: “If it feels good, do it.”
Joseph said: “How could I sin against God?”
Purity is not outdated. It is warfare.
And the terrifying thing is this:
Doing the right thing still got Joseph falsely accused.
Some of you are angry because obedience did not immediately reward you.
But Scripture never promised instant vindication.
Joseph is imprisoned. Again.
Forgotten. Again.
The Hebrew prison term carries the sense of confinement under authority.
Years pass.
Years.
Do not miss this.
God often develops identity in hiddenness before revealing assignment publicly.
The prison was training Joseph for governance.
Pain was teaching him discernment.
Isolation was building endurance.
Humiliation was killing pride.
Then Pharaoh dreams.
And suddenly the gift hidden in Joseph becomes necessary for a nation.
Your calling may feel invisible now. But one day the very thing people ignored may become the answer to someone else’s survival.
Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s dreams.
The wisdom shocks Egypt.
Genesis 41:38 says:
“Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”
The Hebrew phrase:
“רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים” (Ruach Elohim)
The Spirit of God.
Even pagan rulers recognized something supernatural resting on Joseph.
And suddenly the prisoner becomes ruler.
In one day.
Because God can change a life faster than suffering convinced you He could.
But the true untold story of Joseph is not the promotion.
It is the forgiveness.
Because years later the brothers stand before Joseph without recognizing him.
The same brothers. The same betrayal. The same trauma.
And Joseph weeps.
The Hebrew verb:
“בָּכָה” (bakah)
Deep emotional crying. Lamenting. Overwhelming release.
Joseph never became emotionless. Healing did not erase memory.
Some believers think maturity means feeling nothing.
No.
Biblical healing means wounds no longer control your obedience.
Then comes one of the most powerful statements in all of Genesis.
Genesis 50:20:
“But as for you, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good…”
The Hebrew wording is astonishing.
“אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה”
The word “חָשַׁב” (chashav) means: To weave. To plan. To devise. To calculate.
What they designed for destruction… God rewove into deliverance.
That is redemption.
Not denial. Not pretending evil never happened.
Redemption means God is so sovereign He can take human betrayal and still produce purpose.
Joseph’s life ultimately points beyond himself.
Like Joseph, Jesus was beloved by the Father.
Like Joseph, Jesus was rejected by His own.
Like Joseph, Jesus was stripped.
Like Joseph, Jesus was sold for silver.
Like Joseph, Jesus suffered though innocent.
Like Joseph, Jesus descended before being exalted.
And like Joseph, Jesus became the source of salvation for the very people who rejected Him.
The Old Testament was always whispering His name.
Yeshua.
Jesus.
And maybe this is why Joseph’s story still destroys people emotionally.
Because deep down, we are not just reading about Joseph.
We are reading about ourselves.
The pit. The betrayal. The waiting. The loneliness. The silent prayers. The years where heaven seemed quiet.
Some of you are in Genesis 37 right now.
The dream feels attacked.
Some of you are in Genesis 39. Trying to stay pure in a filthy culture.
Some of you are in the prison years. Wondering if God forgot your name.
But Joseph’s story proves something powerful:
God is still working in hidden places.
Your suffering is not always punishment. Sometimes it is preparation.
And one encounter with God can rewrite an entire future.
If Joseph had quit in the pit, Egypt would have starved.
Your survival may be connected to someone else’s deliverance.
Do not surrender your faith because the process hurts.
And maybe tonight, what hurts the most is not what people did to you.
Maybe it is the fear that your life no longer has purpose.
But Joseph’s story screams across generations:
God still writes endings human hands cannot destroy.
Even now.
Especially now.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Some people survived because they discovered God was closest in the seasons that hurt the most.
Filipino Version:
Ang Hindi Naikukuwentong Bahagi ng Buhay ni Jose
May mga kuwento sa Bibliya na madalas nating minamadali.
Nakikita natin ang tagumpay. Naririnig natin ang mga himala. Ipinapangaral natin ang pagtatagumpay.
Pero bihira nating damhin ang bigat ng sakit na dinaanan bago dumating ang tagumpay.
Isa si Jose sa mga taong iyon.
Dahil bago ang palasyo… may hukay.
Bago ang karangalan… may pagtataksil.
Bago ang katuparan ng panaginip… may mga gabing tila tahimik ang langit.
At marahil kaya hanggang ngayon ay tumatagos pa rin ang kuwento niya…
Dahil maraming tao ang marunong maniwala habang maayos ang lahat.
Pero kakaunti ang nananatiling tapat kapag parang iniwan na sila ng Diyos.
Genesis 37:3:
“Minahal ni Israel si Jose nang higit kaysa sa lahat niyang anak…”
Ang salitang Hebreo na ginamit dito ay:
“אָהַב” (ahav)
Hindi lang simpleng pagmamahal. Ito ay malalim na pagmamahal ng tipan. Pagpili. Pabor. Pagkakabit ng puso.
Kita ng lahat ang pabor kay Jose. At minsan… ang pabor ng Diyos sa buhay mo ang mismong dahilan kung bakit ka kinamumuhian ng iba.
Hindi dahil may ginawa kang masama.
Kundi dahil may nakikita silang calling sa’yo na ayaw nilang isuko sa Diyos.
Ang balabal ni Jose ay hindi lang makulay na damit.
Ang “כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים” (ketonet passim) ay malamang simbolo ng dangal, awtoridad, at mana.
Ibig sabihin: May espesyal na layunin si Jose.
At doon nagsimula ang galit.
Genesis 37:4:
“Kinamuhian nila siya at hindi nila siya makausap nang mapayapa.”
Sa Hebreo:
“וְלֹא יָכְלוּ דַּבְּרוֹ לְשָׁלֹם”
Literal: “Hindi nila kayang magsalita ng shalom sa kanya.”
Ang “shalom” ay hindi lang peace.
Ito ay kabuuan. Kapayapaan. Kagalingan. Kaayusan.
Ganito kalala ang inggit.
Kapag nalason ang puso, nawawala ang kakayahang magsalita ng buhay.
At baka may ilan dito na nasugatan ng mga salita ng mga taong puno ng galit.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang mga panaginip.
Ang salitang:
“חֲלוֹם” (chalom)
Ay banal na rebelasyon.
Hindi gawa-gawa ni Jose ang nakita niya. Diyos ang nagpakita.
Pero minsan, kapag bata pa ang pananampalataya, akala natin handa na tayo dahil may natanggap tayong revelation.
Hindi pa alam ni Jose na may timing ang wisdom.
Lalong lumalim ang galit ng kanyang mga kapatid.
Hanggang dumating ang araw na hinubaran siya.
Genesis 37:23:
“Hinubaran nila si Jose ng kanyang balabal…”
Dahil bago sirain ng kaaway ang destiny mo, una niyang aatakihin ang identity mo.
Pagkatapos ay itinapon siya sa hukay.
“בּוֹר” (bor)
Isang malalim na hukay. Lugar ng kadiliman. Pagkakulong. Pagkahiwalay.
At ito ang bahagi ng kuwento na madalas minamadali ng mga sermon.
Labing pitong taong gulang lang si Jose.
Isipin mo iyon.
Siguro sumisigaw siya. Siguro umiiyak. Siguro hinihintay niyang maawa ang mga kapatid niya.
Habang sila… nakaupo at kumakain.
Genesis 37:25:
“At sila’y naupo upang kumain.”
Napakalamig na talata.
Habang si Jose ay nadudurog, normal lang ang araw para sa kanila.
May mga taong ganito rin ang pinagdaanan.
Ikaw ang umiiyak. Pero tuloy lang ang mundo.
Pagkatapos, ipinagbili si Jose bilang alipin.
“עֶבֶד” (eved)
Isang alipin. Pag-aari ng iba.
Mula sa paboritong anak… naging produkto.
Pero kahit ganoon, hindi siya iniwan ng Diyos.
Genesis 39:2:
“At ang Panginoon ay sumasa kay Jose.”
Sa Hebreo:
“וַיְהוָה הָיָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף”
Kasama siya ng Diyos sa pagkaalipin. Kasama siya sa maling paratang. Kasama siya sa kulungan.
Napakahalagang maintindihan ito:
Ang presensya ng Diyos ay hindi nangangahulugang walang paghihirap.
Minsan, pinaka-malapit ang Diyos sa mga panahong halos hindi mo na kaya.
Pagkatapos ay dumating ang tukso.
Inakit si Jose ng asawa ni Potifar.
Pero sinabi ni Jose:
“Paanong gagawin ko ang malaking kasamaan na ito at magkakasala laban sa Diyos?”
Genesis 39:9
Ang “רָעָה” (ra’ah) ay moral na kasamaan.
Hindi ibinase ni Jose ang tama sa kultura. Sa laman. Sa lihim. Sa emosyon.
Ibinase niya ito sa Diyos.
At nakakatakot isipin:
Kahit tama ang ginawa niya, nakulong pa rin siya.
Maraming tao ang nanlamig sa Diyos dahil akala nila ang pagsunod ay laging may instant reward.
Pero hindi iyon ang itinuturo ng Bibliya.
Minsan, ang obedience ay magdadala muna sa’yo sa proseso bago sa promotion.
Lumipas ang mga taon.
Nakalimutan si Jose.
Tahimik. Nakakulong. Naghihintay.
Pero habang akala niya nasasayang ang buhay niya, hinuhubog pala siya ng Diyos.
Ang kulungan ang naghanda sa kanya para mamuno.
Ang sakit ang nagturo ng wisdom.
Ang kahihiyan ang pumatay sa pride.
Pagkatapos, nanaginip si Paraon.
At biglang naging mahalaga ang regalong binale-wala noon.
Minsan, yung bagay na minamaliit ng tao sa’yo ngayon ang magiging dahilan ng pagliligtas ng iba balang araw.
At sa isang iglap, ang preso ay naging pinuno.
Pero ang pinakamakapangyarihang bahagi ng kuwento ni Jose ay hindi ang promotion.
Kundi ang pagpapatawad.
Dahil nang muli niyang makita ang mga kapatid niya, may kapangyarihan na siyang gumanti.
Pero umiyak siya.
“בָּכָה” (bakah)
Malalim na pag-iyak. Paglabas ng matagal nang sakit.
Hindi naging manhid si Jose.
Hindi ibig sabihin ng healing ay wala ka nang nararamdaman.
Ibig sabihin lang: Hindi na kontrolado ng sugat mo ang pagsunod mo sa Diyos.
At pagkatapos ay sinabi niya ang isa sa pinakamagandang linya sa buong Bibliya.
Genesis 50:20:
“Binalak ninyo ang masama laban sa akin, ngunit binalak iyon ng Diyos para sa ikabubuti…”
Ang salitang:
“חָשַׁב” (chashav)
Ay mangahulugang: maghabi, magplano, bumuo.
Yung plano nilang sirain siya… hinabi ng Diyos para maging kaligtasan.
Iyan ang redemption.
Hindi paglimot. Hindi pagdedeny ng sakit.
Kundi ang kakayahan ng Diyos na gawing may layunin kahit ang pinakamadilim na pagtataksil.
At higit sa lahat, ang buhay ni Jose ay larawan ni Cristo.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay minahal ng Ama.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay itinakwil ng sarili Niyang bayan.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay ipinagbili.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay nagdusa kahit inosente.
Tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ay ibinaba bago itinaas.
At tulad ni Jose, si Jesus ang naging daan ng kaligtasan para mismo sa mga taong tumanggi sa Kanya.
Yeshua.
Jesus.
At baka kaya ka tinatamaan ng kuwento ni Jose ngayon…
Dahil hindi mo lang nakikita si Jose.
Nakikita mo ang sarili mo.
Ang paghihintay. Ang sakit. Ang betrayal. Ang tahimik na gabi. Ang mga panahong parang walang sagot ang Diyos.
Pero tandaan mo ito:
Hindi tumitigil ang Diyos gumalaw kahit tahimik Siya.
Ang hukay ay hindi dulo ng kuwento.
At ang proseso ay hindi ebidensya na iniwan ka na ng Diyos.
Kung sumuko si Jose sa hukay, may bansang mamamatay sa gutom.
Maaaring may mga taong nakakabit ang future sa katapatan mo ngayon.
Kaya huwag kang bibitaw.
Kahit pagod ka na. Kahit umiiyak ka na. Kahit hindi mo maintindihan ang ginagawa ng Diyos.
Maging totoo ka. Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Minsan, doon mo mararamdaman na pinakamalapit ang Diyos… sa panahong akala mo iniwan ka na Niya.
